claim: ChAR-seq is a proximity ligation and sequencing method that maps all RNA-to-DNA contacts across the genome.
source: Here, we present a proximity ligation and sequencing method called Chromatin-Associated RNA sequencing (ChAR-seq) that maps all RNA-to-DNA contacts across the genome.
evidence: The abstract directly states the method and its capability.

claim: ChAR-seq provides unbiased, de novo identification of targets of chromatin-bound RNAs including nascent transcripts in Drosophila cells.
source: Using Drosophila cells, we show that ChAR-seq provides unbiased, de novo identification of targets of chromatin-bound RNAs including nascent transcripts, chromosome-specific dosage compensation ncRNAs, and genome-wide trans-associated RNAs involved in co-transcriptional RNA processing.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the study.

claim: ChAR-seq identifies chromosome-specific dosage compensation ncRNAs.
source: Using Drosophila cells, we show that ChAR-seq provides unbiased, de novo identification of targets of chromatin-bound RNAs including nascent transcripts, chromosome-specific dosage compensation ncRNAs, and genome-wide trans-associated RNAs involved in co-transcriptional RNA processing.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this capability of the method.

claim: ChAR-seq identifies genome-wide trans-associated RNAs involved in co-transcriptional RNA processing.
source: Using Drosophila cells, we show that ChAR-seq provides unbiased, de novo identification of targets of chromatin-bound RNAs including nascent transcripts, chromosome-specific dosage compensation ncRNAs, and genome-wide trans-associated RNAs involved in co-transcriptional RNA processing.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding.

claim: Much of the eukaryotic genome is transcribed into non-coding RNA (ncRNA).
source: Much of the eukaryotic genome is transcribed into non-coding RNA (ncRNA), and several studies have established that a subset of these ncRNAs form ribonucleoprotein complexes that bind and regulate chromatin (Guttman and Rinn, 2012; Meller et al., 2015; Cech and Steitz, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A subset of ncRNAs form ribonucleoprotein complexes that bind and regulate chromatin.
source: Much of the eukaryotic genome is transcribed into non-coding RNA (ncRNA), and several studies have established that a subset of these ncRNAs form ribonucleoprotein complexes that bind and regulate chromatin (Guttman and Rinn, 2012; Meller et al., 2015; Cech and Steitz, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: roX1 and roX2 are part of the male-specific lethal (MSL) complex in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, roX1 and roX2 are part of the male-specific lethal (MSL) complex that coats the single male X chromosome to acetylate histone H4K16 and increase transcription (Conrad and Akhtar, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: The MSL complex coats the single male X chromosome to acetylate histone H4K16 and increase transcription.
source: In Drosophila, roX1 and roX2 are part of the male-specific lethal (MSL) complex that coats the single male X chromosome to acetylate histone H4K16 and increase transcription (Conrad and Akhtar, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Xist is expressed from a single X-chromosomal locus in female mammals and coats the X chromosome from which it is expressed to silence transcription.
source: In female mammals, Xist is expressed from a single X-chromosomal locus and coats the X chromosome from which it is expressed in order to silence transcription (Augui et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: HOTAIR has been shown to regulate expression of specific genes by localizing to chromatin and recruiting activating or repressing proteins.
source: Other ncRNAs, such as HOTAIR (Rinn et al., 2007; Chu et al., 2011), HOTTIP (Wang et al., 2011), and enhancer RNAs (Sigova et al., 2015), have been shown to regulate expression of specific genes by localizing to chromatin and recruiting activating or repressing proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HOTTIP has been shown to regulate expression of specific genes by localizing to chromatin and recruiting activating or repressing proteins.
source: Other ncRNAs, such as HOTAIR (Rinn et al., 2007; Chu et al., 2011), HOTTIP (Wang et al., 2011), and enhancer RNAs (Sigova et al., 2015), have been shown to regulate expression of specific genes by localizing to chromatin and recruiting activating or repressing proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Enhancer RNAs have been shown to regulate expression of specific genes by localizing to chromatin and recruiting activating or repressing proteins.
source: Other ncRNAs, such as HOTAIR (Rinn et al., 2007; Chu et al., 2011), HOTTIP (Wang et al., 2011), and enhancer RNAs (Sigova et al., 2015), have been shown to regulate expression of specific genes by localizing to chromatin and recruiting activating or repressing proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Repetitive ncRNA transcripts have roles at telomeres (TERRA).
source: Finally, repetitive ncRNA transcripts have roles at chromosomal loci essential in maintaining genomic integrity over many cell divisions, including TERRA at telomeres (Bunting et al., 2010) and alpha-satellites near centromeres (Hall et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Alpha-satellite ncRNAs have roles near centromeres.
source: Finally, repetitive ncRNA transcripts have roles at chromosomal loci essential in maintaining genomic integrity over many cell divisions, including TERRA at telomeres (Bunting et al., 2010) and alpha-satellites near centromeres (Hall et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The genomic targets of most chromatin-associated ncRNAs are unknown.
source: Despite these well-studied examples, the genomic targets of most chromatin-associated ncRNAs are unknown, and the mechanisms by which these ncRNAs regulate the epigenetic and spatial organization of chromatin remain largely unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: ChIRP, CHART, and RAP are genomic methods for studying the localization of specific RNA transcripts.
source: Genomic methods for studying the localization of specific RNA transcripts include ChIRP (Chu et al., 2011), CHART (Engreitz et al., 2013), and RAP (Simon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous methods.

claim: ChIRP, CHART, and RAP use hybridization of complementary oligonucleotides to pull down a single target RNA.
source: These techniques use hybridization of complementary oligonucleotides to pull down a single target RNA and then next generation sequencing or mass spectrometry to identify its DNA- or protein-binding partners (Simon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing these methods.

claim: De novo discovery of chromatin-associated RNAs remains limited to computational predictions or association with previously known factors.
source: However, de novo discovery of chromatin-associated RNAs remains limited to computational predictions (Guttman and Rinn, 2012) or association with previously known factors (Khalil et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Nuclear fractionation allows isolation of bulk chromatin and subsequent identification of chromatin bound RNAs via sequencing, but does not provide sequence-resolved maps of RNA binding locations along the genome.
source: Nuclear fractionation allows isolation of bulk chromatin and subsequent identification of chromatin bound RNAs via sequencing, but does not provide sequence-resolved maps of RNA binding locations along the genome (Werner and Ruthenburg, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: ChAR-seq was developed and performed using Drosophila melanogaster CME-W1-cl8+ cells.
source: We developed and performed ChAR-seq using Drosophila melanogaster CME-W1-cl8+ cells, a male wing disc derived cell line with a normal karyotype and well-characterized epigenome and transcriptome (Cherbas et al., 2011; Roy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental system used.

claim: CME-W1-cl8+ is a male wing disc derived cell line with a normal karyotype and well-characterized epigenome and transcriptome.
source: We developed and performed ChAR-seq using Drosophila melanogaster CME-W1-cl8+ cells, a male wing disc derived cell line with a normal karyotype and well-characterized epigenome and transcriptome (Cherbas et al., 2011; Roy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous characterization of this cell line.

claim: ChAR-seq is a chromosome conformation capture method that maps genome-wide RNA-to-DNA contacts in crosslinked nuclei.
source: ChAR-seq is a chromosome conformation capture method that maps genome-wide RNA-to-DNA contacts in crosslinked nuclei (Dekker et al., 2002; Rao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct description of the method with citations to related techniques.

claim: The oligonucleotide bridge contains a 5'-adenylated end that ensures it is the only 5' end competent for ligation to the 3'-ends of ssRNA by truncated T4 Rnl2tr R55K K227Q mutant ligase.
source: the 5'-adenylated end (5'App) of the bridge ensures that it is the only 5' end competent for ligation to the 3'-ends of ssRNA by truncated T4 Rnl2tr R55K K227Q mutant ligase (Viollet et al., 2011), which cannot adenylate 5' ends
evidence: This is a description of the bridge design with a citation to the ligase properties.

claim: The truncated T4 Rnl2tr R55K K227Q mutant ligase cannot adenylate 5' ends.
source: the 5'-adenylated end (5'App) of the bridge ensures that it is the only 5' end competent for ligation to the 3'-ends of ssRNA by truncated T4 Rnl2tr R55K K227Q mutant ligase (Viollet et al., 2011), which cannot adenylate 5' ends
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on the ligase.

claim: The bridge sequence does not exist in the yeast, fly, mouse or human genomes.
source: the sequence of the bridge does not exist in the yeast, fly, mouse or human genomes and encodes a defined polarity
evidence: This is a statement about the bridge design.

claim: The bridge is biotinylated so that it can be captured and enriched.
source: the bridge is biotinylated so that it can be captured and enriched
evidence: This is a description of the bridge design feature.

claim: DpnII has a median spacing of ~200 bp between sites in the fly genome.
source: The genomic DNA is then digested using the restriction enzyme DpnII, which has a median spacing of ~200 bp between sites in the fly genome.
evidence: This is a statement about the restriction enzyme properties in the fly genome.

claim: ChAR-seq generated 22.2 million high-confidence unique mapping events for ~16,800 RNA transcripts.
source: After post-processing for unique alignments, repeat removal, and removal of blacklisted regions, each RNA molecule was mapped to the genomic location to which it was ligated (see Materials and methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), resulting in 22.2 million high-confidence unique mapping events for ~16,800 RNA transcripts.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data output from the method.

claim: RNase-treatment reduced the number of unique bridge molecules identified by six-fold.
source: This RNase-treatment reduced the number of unique bridge molecules identified by six-fold, demonstrating that the vast majority of bridge ligation events are indeed RNA-dependent (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from a control experiment.

claim: The ChAR-seq protocol is highly reproducible, with the number normalized RNA-to-DNA contacts observed for each RNA showing high concordance between replicates.
source: The ChAR-seq protocol is highly reproducible, with the number normalized RNA-to-DNA contacts observed for each RNA showing high concordance between replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in a figure supplement.

claim: Even when spike-in RNA was added at 10% of the total soluble RNA, fewer than 0.5% false positive RNA-to-DNA contacts were observed.
source: Though we see a clear concentration-dependent increase in the number of false positives, even in the scenario where we spiked in RNA at 10% of the total soluble RNA we observed fewer than 0.5% false positive RNA-to-DNA contacts (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), which compares favorably to the false positive rates in related RNA-DNA mapping methods (Li et al., 2017; Sridhar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from a spike-in control experiment.

claim: The false positive rate in ChAR-seq compares favorably to the false positive rates in related RNA-DNA mapping methods.
source: Though we see a clear concentration-dependent increase in the number of false positives, even in the scenario where we spiked in RNA at 10% of the total soluble RNA we observed fewer than 0.5% false positive RNA-to-DNA contacts (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), which compares favorably to the false positive rates in related RNA-DNA mapping methods (Li et al., 2017; Sridhar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to other methods with citations.

claim: 85% of the RNAs captured in ChAR-seq were sense-stranded.
source: The majority (85% of total) of the RNAs captured in our assay were sense, with the largest single subtype represented by sense-stranded mRNA (32% of total), owing to the capture of nascent transcripts (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: Sense-stranded mRNA represented 32% of total captured RNAs.
source: The majority (85% of total) of the RNAs captured in our assay were sense, with the largest single subtype represented by sense-stranded mRNA (32% of total), owing to the capture of nascent transcripts (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: 96% of the antisense mRNAs were intronic in origin.
source: In fact, 96% of the antisense mRNAs were intronic in origin with 64% of these originating from a single 119 kb gene (CG42339), suggesting the presence of unannotated ncRNAs in this region.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: 64% of antisense intronic mRNAs originated from a single 119 kb gene (CG42339).
source: In fact, 96% of the antisense mRNAs were intronic in origin with 64% of these originating from a single 119 kb gene (CG42339), suggesting the presence of unannotated ncRNAs in this region.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: The concentration of antisense mRNAs from gene CG42339 suggests the presence of unannotated ncRNAs in this region.
source: In fact, 96% of the antisense mRNAs were intronic in origin with 64% of these originating from a single 119 kb gene (CG42339), suggesting the presence of unannotated ncRNAs in this region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis.

claim: 18% of non-protein coding transcripts detected were small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA).
source: The remaining chromatin-associated RNA detected in our assay arose from non-protein coding transcripts (see Figure 1—figure supplement 7), of which 18% were small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA) and 19% were small nuclear RNA (snRNA).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: 19% of non-protein coding transcripts detected were small nuclear RNA (snRNA).
source: The remaining chromatin-associated RNA detected in our assay arose from non-protein coding transcripts (see Figure 1—figure supplement 7), of which 18% were small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA) and 19% were small nuclear RNA (snRNA).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: Individual RNAs mapped by ChAR-seq generally fell into one of three classes.
source: Individual RNAs mapped by ChAR-seq generally fell into one of three classes.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data classification.

claim: In the first class, RNAs were found around the locus from which they are transcribed.
source: In the first class, RNAs were found around the locus from which they are transcribed (Figure 1C, see, e.g., Hsromega, chinmo, ten-m).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data classification with figure reference.

claim: In the second class, RNAs were found bound to chromatin in trans, generally distributed across most or all of the genome.
source: In the second class, RNAs were found bound to chromatin in trans, generally distributed across most or all of the genome, often in addition to a peak around the gene body from which the RNA is transcribed (Figure 1C, see e.g., snRNA:U2, snRNA:7SK).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data classification with figure reference.

claim: In a third class, RNAs that are part of the dosage compensation complex (roX1 and roX2) were enriched on and coat the X chromosome.
source: In a third class, RNAs that are part of the dosage compensation complex (Figure 1C, see roX1 and roX2) were enriched on and coat the X chromosome.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data classification with figure reference.

claim: Aggregated RNA-to-DNA contacts show qualitative agreement with PRO-seq data.
source: To investigate this first class of RNAs, we compared aggregated RNA-to-DNA contacts with data from nascent transcription sequencing using PRO-seq (Kwak et al., 2013), and observed qualitative agreement between PRO-seq and ChAR-seq data sets (Figure 1D, see PRO-seq and mRNA).
evidence: This is a direct statement of comparison with another method.

claim: Many RNA-to-DNA contacts are associated in trans to genomic regions outside of the gene body from which the RNA is transcribed.
source: Nevertheless, many RNA-to-DNA contacts in our dataset are associated in trans to genomic regions outside of the gene body from which the RNA is transcribed (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: Topologically associated domains (TADs) are preserved in the mock-treated sample.
source: Topologically associated domains (TADs) are preserved in the mock-treated sample and the DNA-DNA contacts show high correlation with previously published CME-W1-cl8+ cell Hi-C (Ramírez et al., 2015) (Figure 1—figure supplements 9–10).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results with citation.

claim: DNA-DNA contacts in the mock-treated sample show high correlation with previously published CME-W1-cl8+ cell Hi-C.
source: Topologically associated domains (TADs) are preserved in the mock-treated sample and the DNA-DNA contacts show high correlation with previously published CME-W1-cl8+ cell Hi-C (Ramírez et al., 2015) (Figure 1—figure supplements 9–10).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results with citation.

claim: The three-dimensional genome organization is largely preserved in the ChAR-seq protocol.
source: Thus, the three-dimensional genome organization is largely preserved in our protocol.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Hi-C comparison data.

claim: The profile of RNA-to-DNA contacts detected by ChAR-seq was distinctly different from that of DNA-to-DNA contacts in the mock-treated Hi-C library.
source: Furthermore, the profile of RNA-to-DNA contacts detected by ChAR-seq was distinctly different from that of DNA-to-DNA contacts in our mock-treated Hi-C library (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 9), indicating that ChAR-seq signal is not simply a byproduct of DNA-DNA contacts.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data comparison results.

claim: ChAR-seq signal is not simply a byproduct of DNA-DNA contacts.
source: Furthermore, the profile of RNA-to-DNA contacts detected by ChAR-seq was distinctly different from that of DNA-to-DNA contacts in our mock-treated Hi-C library (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 9), indicating that ChAR-seq signal is not simply a byproduct of DNA-DNA contacts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison data.

claim: The majority of the RNAs in the ChAR-seq dataset (14,860 out of 16,812, 88%) had fewer than 10 contacts per kilobase million reads (CPKM).
source: The majority of the RNAs in our dataset (14,860 out of 16,812, 88%) had fewer than 10 contacts per kilobase million reads (CPKM) (Figure 2D) and were excluded from further analysis.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: The remaining 1952 RNAs (12%) accounted for 83% (18.5 million) of all chromatin contacts in the ChAR-seq data set.
source: The remaining 1952 RNAs (12%) accounted for 83% (18.5 million) of all chromatin contacts in our data set.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: There is a correlation between RNA expression level and chromatin-RNA contacts.
source: We observed a correlation between RNA expression level and chromatin-RNA contacts; however, a cluster of RNAs clearly generated more chromatin interactions that would be expected from the overall expression levels (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: A cluster of RNAs generated more chromatin interactions than would be expected from the overall expression levels.
source: We observed a correlation between RNA expression level and chromatin-RNA contacts; however, a cluster of RNAs clearly generated more chromatin interactions that would be expected from the overall expression levels (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: 138 RNAs had more than 100 CPKM and were enriched more than ten-fold.
source: Using both the length and read normalized contacts (CPKM) and the fold-enrichment over RNA expression as measured by RNA-seq, we identified 138 RNAs that had more than 100 CPKM and were enriched more than ten-fold, though many were enriched by 2–5 orders of magnitude (Figure 2E, red symbols; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: Many of the 138 highly enriched RNAs were enriched by 2–5 orders of magnitude.
source: Using both the length and read normalized contacts (CPKM) and the fold-enrichment over RNA expression as measured by RNA-seq, we identified 138 RNAs that had more than 100 CPKM and were enriched more than ten-fold, though many were enriched by 2–5 orders of magnitude (Figure 2E, red symbols; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: There is good concordance between the RNAs identified using the enrichment methodology between replicates.
source: Notably, we observe good concordance between the RNAs identified using this methodology between replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: roX1 and roX2 were used as internal positive controls in the male WME-cl8+ line.
source: We developed ChAR-seq using the male WME-cl8+ line, reasoning that the ncRNAs roX1 and roX2 would serve as an internal positive control.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental design rationale.

claim: roX1 was 7.6-fold (p-value<10−10) enriched for interactions on the X chromosome.
source: Indeed, ChAR-seq data showed roX1 and roX2 to be 7.6-fold (p-value<10−10) and 8.1-fold (p-value<10−10) enriched for interactions on the X chromosome, respectively (Figure 3B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results with statistical significance.

claim: roX2 was 8.1-fold (p-value<10−10) enriched for interactions on the X chromosome.
source: Indeed, ChAR-seq data showed roX1 and roX2 to be 7.6-fold (p-value<10−10) and 8.1-fold (p-value<10−10) enriched for interactions on the X chromosome, respectively (Figure 3B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results with statistical significance.

claim: Female flies express Sex lethal (Sxl), which binds to msl2 mRNA to prevent its translation, blocking assembly of the MSL2 complex.
source: In contrast, female flies express Sex lethal (Sxl), which binds to msl2 mRNA to prevent its translation, blocking assembly of the MSL2 complex (Lucchesi and Kuroda, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: roX1 and roX2 require MSL2 for X-chromosome specific localization.
source: Importantly, roX1 and roX2 require MSL2 for X-chromosome specific localization (Lucchesi and Kuroda, 2015), therefore female cells should lack detectable spreading of these ncRNAs along the X-chromosome.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Female cells should lack detectable spreading of roX1 and roX2 along the X-chromosome.
source: Importantly, roX1 and roX2 require MSL2 for X-chromosome specific localization (Lucchesi and Kuroda, 2015), therefore female cells should lack detectable spreading of these ncRNAs along the X-chromosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known biology with citation.

claim: ChAR-seq in female Drosophila melanogaster cell line Kc167 did not detect any significant roX2 localization on the X chromosome.
source: When we performed ChAR-seq in a female Drosophila melanogaster cell line, Kc167, we did not detect any significant roX2 localization on the X chromosome (Figure 3D) but observed excellent agreement in interaction signal from other RNAs across both cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3C male, CME-W1-cl8+ and Figure 3D, female, Kc167, see e.g., snRNA:7SK and Hsromega).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: There was excellent agreement in interaction signal from other RNAs across male and female cell lines.
source: When we performed ChAR-seq in a female Drosophila melanogaster cell line, Kc167, we did not detect any significant roX2 localization on the X chromosome (Figure 3D) but observed excellent agreement in interaction signal from other RNAs across both cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3C male, CME-W1-cl8+ and Figure 3D, female, Kc167, see e.g., snRNA:7SK and Hsromega).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data comparison results.

claim: DNA contact locations for roX1 and roX2 were in surprisingly good agreement between ChIRP-seq and ChAR-seq.
source: Comparing ChIRP-seq to ChAR-seq for both roX1 and roX2 (Figure 3E), we found that DNA contact locations were in surprisingly good agreement despite the fact that ChAR-seq reads are spread across all RNAs while ChIRP-seq reads map the specific RNA target, resulting in a large disparity in the effective sequencing depth between the methods.
evidence: This is a direct statement of comparison results.

claim: In ChAR-seq, roX1 and roX2 represented 0.1% and 0.36% of the dataset, respectively.
source: In the case of roX1 and roX2, we observed 32,308 and 87,453 contacts, representing 0.1% and 0.36% of the ChAR-seq dataset.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: ChAR-seq can identify RNA peaks along chromatin with high sensitivity for a given RNA.
source: This indicates that ChAR-seq can identify RNA peaks along chromatin with high sensitivity for a given RNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison with ChIRP-seq.

claim: ChAR-seq roX1 signal-to-noise ratio was much higher than that of ChIRP-seq (49.8 vs 3.9).
source: We found that ChAR-seq roX1 SNR was much higher than that of ChIRP-seq (49.8 vs 3.9), and ChAR-seq roX2 SNR was about two-fold higher than that of ChIRP-seq (45.2 vs 22.0), despite having 2 orders of magnitude fewer reads in ChAR-seq.
evidence: This is a direct statement of quantitative comparison results.

claim: ChAR-seq roX2 signal-to-noise ratio was about two-fold higher than that of ChIRP-seq (45.2 vs 22.0).
source: We found that ChAR-seq roX1 SNR was much higher than that of ChIRP-seq (49.8 vs 3.9), and ChAR-seq roX2 SNR was about two-fold higher than that of ChIRP-seq (45.2 vs 22.0), despite having 2 orders of magnitude fewer reads in ChAR-seq.
evidence: This is a direct statement of quantitative comparison results.

claim: ChAR-seq has excellent sensitivity and sufficient signal-to-noise to characterize accurate chromatin-binding events for individual RNAs.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that ChAR-seq has excellent sensitivity and sufficient signal-to-noise to characterize accurate chromatin-binding events for individual RNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the signal-to-noise analysis.

claim: The resolution of ChAR-seq is bounded in part by the local DpnII cut frequency and the number of contacts for any given RNA.
source: To measure the accuracy of ChAR-seq measurements of RNA interaction with DNA, we compared ChAR-Seq data to ChIRP-seq data to estimate the base-pair resolution of ChAR-Seq. We expected this resolution to be bounded ––in part––by the local DpnII cut frequency and the number of contacts for any given RNA.
evidence: This is a statement about expected limitations of the method.

claim: ChAR-seq shows a bi-phasic increase of the correlation coefficient with ChIRP-seq, corresponding to a minor plateau around 200 bp and a major plateau at ~25 kbp.
source: Using this method, we noted a bi-phasic increase of the correlation coefficient, corresponding to a minor plateau around 200 bp and a major plateau at ~25 kbp.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: The minor plateau around 200 bp is likely due to the DpnII distribution bias in the ChAR-seq tracks.
source: The minor plateau is likely due to the DpnII distribution bias in the ChAR-seq tracks, while the major plateau is an estimate of the resolution of our assay, which is on the order of other proximity-ligation sequencing assays like Hi-C (van Berkum et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with citation to related methods.

claim: The major plateau at ~25 kbp is an estimate of the resolution of ChAR-seq, which is on the order of other proximity-ligation sequencing assays like Hi-C.
source: The minor plateau is likely due to the DpnII distribution bias in the ChAR-seq tracks, while the major plateau is an estimate of the resolution of our assay, which is on the order of other proximity-ligation sequencing assays like Hi-C (van Berkum et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with citation to related methods.

claim: snRNAs collectively comprised 23% of all the RNA-to-DNA contacts in the ChAR-seq dataset.
source: These snRNAs collectively comprised 23% of all the RNA-to-DNA contacts in our dataset (Figure 4A) and are a substantial component of the spliceosome, a multi-megadalton ribonucleoprotein complex that catalyzes pre-mRNA splicing (Zhou et al., 2002; Will and Lührmann, 2011).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results with citations.

claim: snRNAs are a substantial component of the spliceosome, a multi-megadalton ribonucleoprotein complex that catalyzes pre-mRNA splicing.
source: These snRNAs collectively comprised 23% of all the RNA-to-DNA contacts in our dataset (Figure 4A) and are a substantial component of the spliceosome, a multi-megadalton ribonucleoprotein complex that catalyzes pre-mRNA splicing (Zhou et al., 2002; Will and Lührmann, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Two dominant spliceosome species exist in eukaryotes: the major spliceosome comprised of U1, U2, U4, U5 and U6 snRNAs, and the minor spliceosome comprised of U4:atac, U6:atac, U5, U11, and U12.
source: The composition and conformation of the spliceosome is highly dynamic, though two dominant species exist in eukaryotes: the major spliceosome comprised of U1, U2, U4, U5 and U6 snRNAs, and the minor spliceosome comprised of U4:atac, U6:atac, U5, U11, and U12 (Will and Lührmann, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The distribution patterns of the major spliceosome snRNAs U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 clustered together along with snRNA:7SK.
source: When we then correlated genome-wide binding signal within this class, we found that the distribution patterns of the major spliceosome snRNAs U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 clustered together along with snRNA:7SK (Figure 4B), which is part of the p-TEFb complex that relieves pausing of RNA Polymerase II at promoters (Kwak and Lis, 2013) and may participate in the release of paused polymerase during RNA splicing (Barboric et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results with citations.

claim: snRNA:7SK is part of the p-TEFb complex that relieves pausing of RNA Polymerase II at promoters.
source: When we then correlated genome-wide binding signal within this class, we found that the distribution patterns of the major spliceosome snRNAs U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 clustered together along with snRNA:7SK (Figure 4B), which is part of the p-TEFb complex that relieves pausing of RNA Polymerase II at promoters (Kwak and Lis, 2013) and may participate in the release of paused polymerase during RNA splicing (Barboric et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: snRNA:7SK may participate in the release of paused polymerase during RNA splicing.
source: When we then correlated genome-wide binding signal within this class, we found that the distribution patterns of the major spliceosome snRNAs U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 clustered together along with snRNA:7SK (Figure 4B), which is part of the p-TEFb complex that relieves pausing of RNA Polymerase II at promoters (Kwak and Lis, 2013) and may participate in the release of paused polymerase during RNA splicing (Barboric et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The components of the minor spliceosome did not cluster together, likely due to their low abundance and consequently low representation in the dataset.
source: The components of the minor spliceosome did not cluster together, likely due to their low abundance (Will and Lührmann, 2011) and consequently low representation in our dataset.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with citation.

claim: Spliceosomal RNAs should be enriched in regions of active transcription.
source: We next reasoned that spliceosome RNAs––as part of the co-transcriptional RNA processing machinery––should also be enriched in regions of active transcription.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known biology.

claim: An enrichment of snRNAs (7SK, U2 and U6) was observed over gene bodies with a broad peak around transcription start sites.
source: We observed an enrichment of snRNAs (7SK, U2 and U6), but not roX1 or roX2, over gene bodies (Figure 4C) with a broad peak around transcription start sites, in good agreement with ChIRP data for 7SK in mice (Flynn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results with citation.

claim: The enrichment of snRNAs over gene bodies is in good agreement with ChIRP data for 7SK in mice.
source: We observed an enrichment of snRNAs (7SK, U2 and U6), but not roX1 or roX2, over gene bodies (Figure 4C) with a broad peak around transcription start sites, in good agreement with ChIRP data for 7SK in mice (Flynn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work with citation.

claim: Active transcription is correlated with topological boundaries in flies.
source: Because active transcription is also correlated with topological boundaries in flies (Hou et al., 2012; Ulianov et al., 2016), we examined the relationship between RNA contacts and genome organization.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both 7SK and U2 RNAs were modestly, but significantly enriched at TAD boundaries.
source: Both 7SK and U2 RNAs were modestly, but significantly (Wilcoxon rank-sum test) enriched at TAD boundaries (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A (top)).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results with statistical test.

claim: 7SK and U2 RNAs were ~1.4 fold enriched over TAD boundaries.
source: We also aggregated 7SK and U2 contact signals across all TAD boundaries (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A (bottom), red lines) and a random distribution of identically sized genomic bins (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A (bottom), black lines), and found that these RNAs were ~1.4 fold enriched over boundaries.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: roX2 was ~2.2 fold enriched over TAD boundaries on the X chromosome.
source: We also noted that roX2 was ~2.2 fold enriched over TAD boundaries on the X chromosome (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), consistent with previous data showing that MSL2 dosage compensation complex High Affinity Sites (HAS) are preferentially found at TAD boundaries (Ramírez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results with citation.

claim: MSL2 dosage compensation complex High Affinity Sites (HAS) are preferentially found at TAD boundaries.
source: We also noted that roX2 was ~2.2 fold enriched over TAD boundaries on the X chromosome (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), consistent with previous data showing that MSL2 dosage compensation complex High Affinity Sites (HAS) are preferentially found at TAD boundaries (Ramírez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Open chromatin is enriched at TAD boundaries.
source: Examination of chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) over TAD boundaries (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) showed that open chromatin is enriched at TAD boundaries, supporting the idea that TAD boundaries are transcriptionally active in flies.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: TAD boundaries are transcriptionally active in flies.
source: Examination of chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) over TAD boundaries (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) showed that open chromatin is enriched at TAD boundaries, supporting the idea that TAD boundaries are transcriptionally active in flies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ATAC-seq data.

claim: There are more than 200 snoRNAs in flies.
source: In contrast to the small number of well-defined and well-characterized snRNAs involved in splicing, there are more than 200 snoRNAs in flies (Huang et al., 2005) that are significantly divergent in sequence and, surprisingly, were highly represented in our dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 7 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: snoRNAs were highly represented in the ChAR-seq dataset.
source: In contrast to the small number of well-defined and well-characterized snRNAs involved in splicing, there are more than 200 snoRNAs in flies (Huang et al., 2005) that are significantly divergent in sequence and, surprisingly, were highly represented in our dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 7 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: Most snoRNAs have either unknown function or are computationally identified and indirectly implicated in the maturation and modification of ribosomal rRNA.
source: Most of these snoRNAs have either unknown function or are computationally identified and indirectly implicated in the maturation and modification of ribosomal rRNA (Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: roX1 and roX2 clustered with known dosage compensation complex factors, MOF, the histone modifications H4K16ac and H3K36me3, and JIL-1 kinase.
source: We observed discrete clustering of roX1 and roX2 with known dosage compensation complex factors, MOF, the histone modifications H4K16ac and H3K36me3 (Bell et al., 2008), and JIL-1 kinase (Bai et al., 2004), validating this analytical approach (Figure 4D).

claim: The clustering of roX1 and roX2 with known dosage compensation factors validates the analytical approach.
source: We observed discrete clustering of roX1 and roX2 with known dosage compensation complex factors, MOF, the histone modifications H4K16ac and H3K36me3 (Bell et al., 2008), and JIL-1 kinase (Bai et al., 2004), validating this analytical approach (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data analysis results.

claim: Chromatin-associated RNAs fell into two distinct and anti-correlated categories: those associated with active chromatin and transcription or heterochromatin.
source: Beyond this sub-cluster of dosage compensation factors, the remainder of the chromatin-associated RNAs fell into two distinct and anti-correlated categories: those associated with active chromatin and transcription (e.g., RNAPII, H4K8ac, H3K18ac) or heterochromatin (e.g., HP2, H3K9me3, HP1a) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: snRNA:U2 and snRNA:7SK cluster tightly with the transcription-associated chromatin marks.
source: In particular, we note that snRNA:U2 and snRNA:7SK cluster tightly with the transcription-associated chromatin marks, while many of the snoRNAs and minor spliceosome snRNAs that we identified are associated with heterochromatin, likely due to co-localization of heterochromatin factors to the nucleolus.
evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results.

claim: Many of the snoRNAs and minor spliceosome snRNAs are associated with heterochromatin, likely due to co-localization of heterochromatin factors to the nucleolus.

evidence: This is a direct statement of data analysis results with interpretation.

claim: snRNA:U5 has variants that clearly cluster with either transcriptionally active chromatin (63BC) or heterochromatin (23D, 38ABa, and 34A).
source: Interestingly, snRNA:U5, a component of both the major and minor spliceosome, has variants that clearly cluster with either transcriptionally active chromatin (63BC) or heterochromatin (23D, 38ABa, and 34A).

claim: The snRNA:U5:38Aba variant exhibits a unique tissue-specific expression profile with the greatest abundance in neural tissue.
source: Previous work has shown that the snRNA:U5:38Aba variant (Figure 4D, heterochromatin cluster) exhibits a unique tissue-specific expression profile with the greatest abundance in neural tissue, which led the authors to propose isoform-dependent functions in alternative splicing (Chen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The differential clustering observed for snRNA:U5 might reflect isoform-specific functions of the spliceosome in different chromatin states.
source: The differential clustering that we observe for snRNA:U5, and between major and minor spliceosome snRNAs, for euchromatin and heterochromatin might reflect such isoform-specific functions of the spliceosome in different chromatin states.

source: First, proximity ligations are performed in situ in intact nuclei, which reduces nonspecific interactions (Rao et al., 2014).
